target_audience: University students or advanced high school students (Calculus I)

sections.title: Prerequisite: Functions as Mappings
sections.content: Introduce the idea that a function f(x) is not just a static curve, but a mapping from an 'Input Number Line' to an 'Output Number Line'. Visualize two parallel horizontal lines. When a point moves on the input line, its 'shadow' moves on the output line.
sections.example: Imagine a 'Stretch-Bot' robot. If the input is its position on a ruler, the output is where its laser pointer hits a wall. As it walks, the laser moves at different speeds depending on the wall's angle.

sections.title: Local Linearity: The 'Infinite Zoom'
sections.content: Explain that if we zoom in close enough to any smooth point on a function, the transformation looks like a simple linear stretch or squish. This is the foundation of the derivative as a local property.
sections.example: Visualize a tiny 'Ant' standing at point x on the input line. Zoom in until the curved function f(x) looks like a straight line. The derivative at that point describes exactly what happens to the Ant's small steps.

sections.title: The Derivative as a Scaling Factor
sections.content: Define the derivative f'(x) not as a slope, but as the 'Local Scaling Factor'. If the input space moves by a tiny amount (dx), the output space moves by f'(x) times that amount (df). Mathematical link: df = f'(x) * dx.
sections.example: If f'(x) = 3, think of a small segment on the input line. When mapped to the output line, this segment is stretched to 3 times its original length. If f'(x) = 0.5, the segment is squished to half its size.

sections.title: Visualizing Signs and Magnitudes
sections.content: Explain the physical meaning of the derivative's value in a transformational context. A positive value preserves orientation; a negative value flips the number line; a zero value collapses the segment to a point.
sections.example: Use a 'Rubber Band' analogy. A derivative of -2 means the rubber band is stretched to twice its length AND flipped backward. A derivative of 0 means that specific spot is 'frozen' or momentarily 'pinched'.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Dynamic Derivative
sections.content: Summarize by moving through the entire domain. Show how the 'Scaling Factor' changes continuously, creating a dance of stretching and squishing across the number line. This provides a dynamic intuition for the Chain Rule and Jacobian matrices later on.
sections.example: Animate a character 'Slimey' moving along the x-axis. As Slimey passes through regions where the derivative is high, his 'shadow' on the y-axis moves extremely fast (stretched). When the derivative is near zero, his shadow barely crawls (squished).
